verdict: Clean. Reads as a person who has read the sources and is thinking about them, not as a machine. Literal checks pass: no forbidden word or phrase, no em-dash, both exclamation points are inside John 20:28, no title, years, book count or denomination claim beyond the allowed 'I pastor a Baptist church', criticism lands on right and left in the same paragraph, headings are plain. Six small findings, none 'must': one muddled comparison in the opening, one slogan closer, one stock metaphor, one reply to an objection the essay never voiced, one loose 'Arius sounds sensible', and a date-led chronicle run. Voice is 8 rather than 10 only because the long historical middle could be any careful historian; it becomes unmistakably his from the banquet scene on.

findings.quote: That question matters to ordinary faith more than most people expect, and Constantine's first instinct, that this was a quarrel over words, sounds a good deal more like many American Christians than anything the bishops said.
findings.tell: Vague framing sentence with a comparison that does not parse
findings.why: An instinct is compared to 'many American Christians' and then to 'anything the bishops said'; the two halves of the comparison are different kinds of thing. A reader has to rebuild the sentence to get the point, which is the essay's thesis.
findings.replacement: That question matters to ordinary faith more than most people expect. And many American Christians sound a good deal more like Constantine, who took it for a quarrel over words, than like the bishops.

findings.quote: Some resisted *homoousios* because they feared it erased the difference between the Father and the Son. The history is messier than the Sunday school version.
findings.tell: Paragraph ends by restating itself as a slogan
findings.why: The paragraph has just shown the mess with Hanson and the non-Arian 'Arians'. The closer adds nothing and 'the Sunday school version' is a stock phrase.
findings.replacement: Some resisted *homoousios* because they feared it erased the difference between the Father and the Son.

findings.quote: And if anyone bent the gospel to fit Greek philosophy, Arius is at least as easy to accuse.
findings.tell: Answers an objection the essay never stated
findings.why: The Case Against section raises the emperor, the unscriptural word, the lost writings, the winners' histories and Ehrman. It never raises Greek philosophy, so this paragraph answers a charge out of nowhere; it reads like a point carried in from an outline.
findings.replacement: People also say a Greek word like that bent the gospel to fit philosophy. If anyone did that, Arius is at least as easy to accuse.

findings.tell: Stock metaphor where he would use a plain phrase
findings.why: The surrounding prose is plain ('The emperor's favor did not stay put'); 'the tide turned' is the one ready-made phrase in the section.

findings.quote: To them Arius sounds sensible. In the 320s plenty of bishops thought so too.
findings.why: The Americans just described have never heard of Arius, so he cannot sound like anything to them; and 'sounds sensible' follows 'still sounds reasonable' four sentences earlier.
findings.replacement: Arius would make sense to them. In the 320s he made sense to plenty of bishops too.

findings.quote: Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328. In 335 a council at Tyre deposed him, and Constantine sent him into exile at Trier, in Gaul.
findings.tell: Run of date-led sentences of the same medium length
findings.why: The paragraph is six chronicle sentences in a row, each opening on a date or a name. It is the one place the essay reads like a reference entry.
findings.replacement: Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328, and in 335 a council at Tyre deposed him and Constantine sent him into exile at Trier, in Gaul.

strengths: The frame is earned: Constantine's 'truly idle question' opens the essay and returns as 'Of all the documents in this story, Constantine's letter sounds most like us.'
Arius gets his real case, in his own words and with his own proof texts, before anyone answers him.
'Most of those charges hold.' The concession to the skeptic is plain and specific, and the reply uses evidence (the palace favored Nicaea's opponents for decades).
The essay refuses the triumphant version twice: the emperor's letter on the Jews, and 'The law that enforced it was something else.'
Self-implication is done, not announced: 'Jesus the example is easier to preach than God come down to save us, because an example asks only for effort.'
Sources work as witnesses; each historian is dated and placed (Socrates a century later, Philostorgius on Arius's side), and Hanson and Ehrman each carry an idea.
Contractions appear where speech would have them (isn't, shouldn't, hasn't), and the ending lands on John 1 without a recap.
for_james: Your saved Substack profile and docs/VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md disagree, and I followed VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md. The profile asks for 1,500 to 2,500 words, paragraphs of two to four sentences, a 'Monday Morning' block of three questions and one practice, a screenshot line, and no exclamation marks ever. This essay runs about 3,700 words in developed paragraphs, ends without an application box, and keeps the exclamation in Thomas's words (John 20:28) because it is verbatim Scripture.

The essay is yours from the banquet scene onward; the historical middle could be any careful historian. The one thing that would close that gap is a real memory only you can supply. The Case Against Nicaea section is the natural place: if, as an atheist, you once believed that Constantine invented the divinity of Jesus, one plain sentence saying so would do it. Nothing has been invented, and nothing should be.

'A carpenter makes a table ... A father begets a son' follows the making-and-begetting illustration C. S. Lewis uses in Mere Christianity (his example is a statue, not a table). The wording is not his, but you may want to credit him or keep it as is.
'I pastor a Baptist church' is the essay's only biographical line. It is used to put your own tradition under the argument, not as a credential, so I left it.
